title: Search inside an inventory tool
metaTitle: Search in the words on the box
excerpt: Floor staff search when aisle names and the app disagree. Show matches in the words on the box, and return them to the count without losing the quantity they typed.
alt: Three pale speckled bottles on a gray surface, two holding dried seed heads, objects you would look up by the name on the vessel.
caption: You would search for what is written on the thing, not for a hidden code. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Why does the floor search an inventory tool?
faqs.answer: They search when navigation failed. The aisle label does not match the app's category, the pick path sent them wrong, or they have a supplier name and the task has an internal code. Search should accept the words printed on the box and the bin code painted on the rack.

faqs.question: What should a search result show on the floor?
faqs.answer: Show the name on the carton, the bin, and whether they can count it. One result they can scan or confirm is better than a table of columns. If several bins match, list the bins in the order of the building, not in a relevance score they cannot see.

faqs.question: What happens to an in-progress count?
faqs.answer: It stays. Searching must not clear the quantity they typed or the line they were on. Return them to that line with the number intact. A search that abandons a count is how the same bin gets entered twice, or not at all.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Inventory tool search UX is what the person on the floor uses when the aisle and the app disagree. They are not browsing a catalog from a chair. Show matches in the language printed on the box, and give them a way back to the count without losing the quantity they typed.

If search speaks only in internal ids, they will walk the aisle twice and then trust the carton. The carton is in their hand. Your id is not. The result row has to take their side.

## They search because the path failed

The pick path failed. The category they were given is a buying-team name, and the rack is labeled with a bin. The barcode is scuffed. Someone on the radio used a supplier nickname. Any of these send a person to the search field, often with a glove on and the count half done.

Put the field on the task screen, not inside a back-office menu. A hardware scanner button and a type-in field can share one results list. They will switch between scan and search in the same minute. Forcing a mode change loses the thread.

Keep the current line on screen while they search, even if it shrinks to a bar. "Counting bin C4, quantity 12, not confirmed." That bar is the landmark. If the search replaces it with no trace, they will confirm the wrong bin when they tap back in a hurry.

Nielsen's research for the Nielsen Norman Group says people often abandon a page in 10 to 20 seconds when the point is not obvious. A floor search has less time than that. [How long people stay on a page](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is a fair warning against a results view that leads with filters, photos of the warehouse, and a featured product. Lead with bins.

## Matches in the words on the carton

Index the printed name, the bin code, the last digits of the barcode, and the supplier name the floor actually says. You can keep the internal id. You should not require it. A search for the first words on the label should hit, even if the official title adds a size and a color after those words.

Show three facts on each row. The printed name. The bin, in the building's order. Whether they may count it. A held bin stays in the list with the hold sentence you already use elsewhere. Hiding it makes the search disagree with the rack in front of them. They will believe the rack.

Order multiple bins the way the building is walked, not by a score. Aisle 4 before Aisle 9 if that is the path. If you do not know the path, order by bin code and say the code clearly. A "best match" that jumps them across the building is a long walk for a typo.

Photos help when they are photos of the real product. A placeholder graphic does not. If the photo is wrong, it will beat the name in their attention and they will pick the wrong row. No photo is better than a wrong one.

Do not show cost, margin, or on-hand value on a floor result. Those are office columns. They clutter the row and they leak. Quantity on hand can show if the floor is allowed to see it. If they are not, say hidden, do not leave a blank that looks like zero. Zero is a number they will act on.

## A way back that preserves the count

This is the rule that keeps the ledger honest. Search is a detour from a line. The detour ends at the same line, with the same unconfirmed quantity.

The query remains in the field until they clear it. They edit "blu" into "blue lid" with a thumb. Clearing on submit makes them retype, and retyping is when they accept a fuzzy match they did not mean.

Back from a result returns to the count, not to a home dashboard. The button can say the bin they were on. If they choose a new bin from the results, ask before you throw away an unconfirmed quantity. "Leave C4 without confirming 12?" Yes or stay. Silent discard is a lost count. Silent keep, attached to the wrong bin, is a wrong count. Ask.

If they had not typed a quantity yet, switching bins can be immediate. The danger is the half-finished line. Design for that state specifically. It is the state they are in when they search, because they searched when the line confused them.

Do not auto-correct a bin code without showing it. Bin codes that differ by one character are different places. Offer the neighbor as a second row. Do not replace C4 with C5 in the field on your own. They will confirm C5 and walk away from C4.

## Nothing matched, and the carton is still in their hand

Repeat the query. "No bin or item matches 'blue lid.'" Offer scan, and offer flag for the office. Do not create an item from the query. Creating master data from a misspelled search is how catalogs fill with ghosts.

If the match failed because of a zone permission, use the permission sentence. Do not say "no match" for a bin they are not allowed to count. They can see the bin. The rack is a better witness than your empty state. "Blue lid is in C4. You can look, you cannot count it. Ask a lead." That is a match with a rule.

If the network is down and search cannot run, say whether the on-device list is complete. A partial cache that pretends to be the warehouse will hide bins that arrived yesterday. "Search on this device may be missing today's receipts" is an honest limit. A spinning wheel with no local fallback strands them in the aisle.

Do not fill an empty search with popular items or recently sold items. This is not a shop. A suggested product they did not type is a trap. They will tap it because it is the only tap, and the count will name the wrong goods.


## Scan, type, and the scuffed label

The floor will mix a scan and typing in one lookup. A scuffed barcode fails, they type the last digits, and the list should treat that as search, not as a separate mode with a different way back. One results list, one return to the count. If scan and search keep two histories, they will confirm a bin from the history they did not mean, and the quantity they typed will follow the wrong row.

Recent bins they counted today can sit under an empty field, labeled as theirs, not as popular stock. Popular stock is an office idea. Their last few bins are a memory aid when the radio interrupted them. Clear that list at the end of the shift, or when the user changes. The next person on the device should not inherit a map of someone else's round. Inheritance like that is how a permission boundary fails without a single role being wrong.

Partial codes need a limit you can explain. Matching a few digits across a whole warehouse can return a pile of bins. Say how many you found, and show the aisle on every row so they can stand still and discard the ones that are a building away. If the pile is large, ask for one more character instead of dumping a long list they cannot scroll with one hand. A long list on a phone in a glove is not a result. It is another aisle to walk, on glass.

Sorting by distance only helps if you know where they are standing. A wrong beacon that sorts the far aisle first is worse than plain bin order. If you are not confident in the location, use bin order and say that in a quiet line under the field. A feature you cannot trust should not be allowed to reorder a count.
## Review it mid-count

Start a count, type a quantity, do not confirm, then search for a supplier nickname, a partial bin, and a scuffed barcode's last four digits. Each result should be readable one-handed. Returning without choosing should restore the quantity. Choosing a different bin should ask before discarding it.

Run the same search as a floor user and as the office. The office can see more columns. The floor should not see a different existence of bins. Held stock is visible to both, with the floor's actions limited. If the office search finds it and the floor search does not, you will get a radio call you could have replaced with a row.

Settings are the next cabinet, and they are easy to overbuild. The floor changes zone, type size, and scanner sound. Almost nothing else. That piece is [settings in an inventory tool](/blog/settings-in-an-inventory-tool). Search that ignores the zone they set will look broken when it is only looking in the wrong aisle.

If the floor's lookup should return a bin they can act on, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). A search box in the header is not the feature. The feature is the trip back to an unconfirmed count that is still true.
